content: Virola, also referred to as Epená, is a genus of medium-sized trees that are indigenous to the South American rainforest. These trees are closely related to other members of the Myristicaceae family, such as nutmeg. The trees are characterized by their glossy, dark leaves and clusters of small yellow flowers. They emit a strong, distinctive odor. The bark of Virola trees produces a dark-red resin that contains several hallucinogenic alkaloids. Among these are 5-MeO-DMT (found in Virola calophylla), 5-OH-DMT (commonly known as bufotenine), and N,N-DMT, which is considered one of the most potent compounds in the dimethyltryptamine family. Additionally, the resin contains beta-carboline harmala alkaloids, which act as monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) and significantly enhance the effects of DMT. The resin is typically processed and dried using various methods. These methods often involve the addition of ash or lime, which are believed to act as basifying agents, as well as a powdered preparation made from the leaves of the Justicia bush. The resulting preparation is consumed in a manner similar to Yopo, involving assisted insufflation. In this process, the snuff is blown through a long tube into the nostrils by another individual. Ethnobotanist Richard Evans Schultes documented that the use of Virola in magico-religious rituals is limited to certain indigenous tribes residing in the Western Amazon Basin and parts of the Orinoco Basin. In the context of traditional medicine, the tops of Virola oleifera have been found to produce compounds such as lignan-7-ols and verrucosin, which exhibit antifungal properties. These compounds have demonstrated efficacy against Cladosporium sphaerospermum at doses as low as 25 micrograms. Furthermore, lignan-7-ols, specifically oleiferin-B and oleiferin-G, have shown activity against Cladosporium cladosporoides at doses starting from 10 micrograms.
